content: During treatment with a daily dose of 25 mg/kg of ethambutol, monthly eye examinations are recommended to monitor for potential visual side effects. For patients who have previously undergone antituberculous therapy, ethambutol should be administered at a dose of 25 mg/kg (11 mg/lb) of body weight as a single oral dose every 24 hours. It is essential to concurrently administer at least one other antituberculous drug to which the causative organisms have demonstrated susceptibility through appropriate in vitro testing. These additional drugs should ideally not have been used previously in the patient’s treatment regimen. After 60 days of therapy, the ethambutol dose should be reduced to 15 mg/kg (7 mg/lb) of body weight, administered as a single oral dose every 24 hours. For adults, the standard dose is 15 mg/kg orally once daily, combined with other antituberculous drugs, with a maximum daily dose not exceeding 1 gram. Ethambutol is not recommended for use as a standalone treatment, either in initial therapy or retreatment. Ethambutol therapy should be continued until bacteriological conversion is permanent and maximal clinical improvement has been achieved. The drug is primarily excreted by the kidneys, and patients with reduced renal function require dosage adjustments based on serum drug levels. Baseline and periodic assessments of organ function, including renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic systems, are advised during treatment. Ethambutol may cause optic neuritis, which can manifest as decreased visual acuity, color blindness, or other visual defects. These effects are generally reversible upon prompt discontinuation of the drug, although irreversible blindness has been reported in rare cases. Patients with pre-existing visual defects, such as cataracts, optic neuritis, or diabetic retinopathy, may experience difficulty in evaluating changes in vision due to underlying conditions. In such cases, the potential benefits of treatment should be carefully weighed against the risk of visual deterioration. Liver toxicity, including fatalities, has been reported with ethambutol use. Baseline and periodic liver function tests are recommended. The drug is not recommended for pediatric patients under 13 years of age, as safety conditions for this age group have not been established. Ethambutol may interact with other medications. For example, it can decrease the efficacy of the BCG vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism and may reduce the effects of uric acid-lowering agents like allopurinol, febuxostat, and probenecid, potentially leading to hyperuricemia and gout. Dosage adjustments of these agents may be necessary. Additionally, aluminum hydroxide-containing antacids can increase ethambutol levels by binding in the gastrointestinal tract. To avoid this interaction, such antacids should not be administered within four hours of an ethambutol dose. Common side effects of ethambutol include headache, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and upset stomach. Rare but serious allergic reactions may occur. Patients should report any symptoms of hypersensitivity, such as rash, itching, or difficulty breathing, to their healthcare provider immediately. During pregnancy, ethambutol should only be used when clearly needed, as it crosses the placenta. It also passes into breast milk but is considered compatible with breastfeeding by the American Academy of Pediatrics. However, caution is advised, particularly in mothers with HIV, as breast milk can transmit the virus. Patients should take ethambutol exactly as prescribed, at evenly spaced intervals, and complete the full course of therapy even if symptoms improve. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Ethambutol should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and discarded properly when expired or no longer needed. Patients should maintain all scheduled medical appointments and consult their healthcare provider for any concerns or questions about their treatment.
